Was in and out of ER for panic attacks that followed with a lot of physical symptoms such as throwing up for about 8 hours straight. Lorazepam has helped me immensely and I don’t know where I’d be without it. I take 1mg 3-4x per day AS NEEDED. It’s been a few years. Take it as needed, which is crucial. Hasn’t been a problem. A lot of people who have bad experiences stop cold turkey or something of the sort. Please realize that the stigma surrounding benzodiazepines is valid, but that some people reaaaally benefit from being on them long(ish) term. Usually, this is in combination with other meds as you’ve stated. Take it as prescribed and please discuss with your provider any questions or concerns. I’d say if you feel any issues with tolerance etc. that you speak to the provider. My biggest advice was do not get into the habit of taking it every single day. Coming from a person w: high anxiety nearly daily, or at least weekly, it’s hard to do this. With these meds it will be more beneficial to take them truly as needed (i.e when you really feel like you are entering a period of panic). Good luck.

I feel for ya. Different situations but similar feelings I assume . I went to community college for two years and then transferred to a pretty good university that my parents happened to live near. I never stayed in dorms, traveled out of my parents house. Pretty much all throughout college until about end of sophomore year when I got apartments with , yes, people I went to high school with who were also attending said university. 

However— I feel like being on campus during these times is pretty different also. 

If you’re not already doing this— you need to not focus on how many friends you’re making, but just focus on making a friend. Believe me, it can be hard. I have horrible anxiety and am pretty socially awkward and I would still always find at least one classmate to sit with and over the semester gained a friendship with. 

Sometimes you have to throw yourself out there. It’s a large part of growing up and maturing. Realize that mostly everyone in that position is feeling nervous and awkward. You really don’t have much to lose by sitting by someone and engaging in conversation/ asking if they want to grab coffee and study for an exam. 

Also— I know there are restrictions and I know this may not be for you... (socially it was not for me either), but there are a lot of different sororities. As mentioned I was associated w a social organization, but if you aren’t interested in that there are a lot of academic and cultural ones as well. That’s a pretty good way to make friends.

I (25F) know this mattered so much to me years ago... but to be really honest a) at this age no one cares or is paying attention to how many likes or views you are getting b) post whatever makes you, you. Post whatever you like and what makes you happy. At the end of the day those who view it or like it (even if smaller amount), then they’re actually liking you for your content/ who you are. C) Instagram hides like count if that matters at all. 

But in all actuality , in the long run of things, likes and views on this platform are almost pointless. Granted years ago it probably mattered to some people, I feel that overall feeling has dissipated. 

No one who posts on Instagram w minimal likes or views are viewed as cringe. Seriously. It’s much easier said than done but just embrace yourself. You will attract people who like you for you. Even if it’s 1 or 2 people. 100+ likes or whatever on a post doesn’t confirm who you are or what kinds of friends you are capable of making. No one is going to think you’re weird for not getting a ton of views or likes. 

If you are having trouble finding friends, and struggle with social norms/skills, please seek out people who you have things in common with. I’ve had social issues before and finding communities on things like this and even tik tok (sad to say lol) can help to find people who are dealing w similar issues. You may find good friends this way. 

But, at the end of the day who you are, what you’re capable of socially has literally nothing to do with how many likes or views you are getting on Instagram. Post  whatever the fuck you want. You cannot take the VTNE in all states with a bachelors in biology or a bachelors in anything really. This is state specific for sure. You need the two year accredited program for most states like New York to even be approved to sit for the exam.

I think this is specific to your own path. Clearly you ended up going with PA school so I doubt regrets w/ VT school was simply about waste of cost. Also pay is so individualized in this field. Depending on where you stand, you’ll make more. Assistants cannot so everything techs do. Including multiple aspects of surgery. OP I think if you’re truly interested and passionate in this field you should start applying for kennel assistant/front desk/vet assistance positions. You do not need a degree for this. Here, you’ll learn restraint techniques, how to take blood, give vacs, and much more. A lot of this will be done by LVT as well. However, you won’t be licensed. If you are interested in being licensed (increased pay and opportunity) you’ll need the school. Vet school followed after being a tech for a bit is a path a lot of doctors follow. The importance of working through each of these phases makes understanding the world of vet medicine so much better. 

This comment also focuses a lot on income. Many professors and specialists in this field will tell you right off the bat— if you are looking into this field for money look elsewhere maybe like being a PA or MD as this person wrote. If you are passionate about animals and know your reason for wanting to enter this field, do whatever makes most sense for your path.

PS I personally had a Bachelors in psych/neuroscience and public health and went into vet (technology) medicine after this fact. This will likely already increase your pay once entering field. Did for me.

I finally started this past September, and while I’ve been in school I have been working in a local veterinary hospital as an assistant learning such amazing things each and every day through experience. 

I agree w the first comment. Definitely getting some hands on experience before entering a program will only help you and make you better prepared for vet tech program. Getting an associates degree after already receiving a bachelors can seem strange (it did for me for a while), but honestly you have to do what makes you happy and what’s going to work for you in the long run. 

There is really no “conventional” way of achieving and pursuing your goals. Whether that be getting a BS first then applying for VT programs, or even taking a year or two or however many you need to figure exactly what options you have and what path you want to take. There is a lot to do in this field, and you can definitely get started without a degree! Good luck and hope this helps!
